#45430. Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (296 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems.
  • It has been revealed that as we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems.
  • We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through Daybreak Red.

It has been revealed that as we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we declared that Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint. We also raised our bug bounty rewards to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed.

We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us. The team builds AI agents for code review, penetration testing, and red teaming. Their research⁠(opens in a new window) has uncovered vulnerabilities in how applications, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems interact. Their work reveals what’s possible when security engineers build around AI to move faster and take on more ambitious research.

In a recent development, as AI agents connect services in new ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.

We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our people. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our Security Bug Bounty program⁠(opens in a new window).

How VistaPrint helps small businesses get the word out

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Small business owners preparing for a launch or an event often know what they want to accomplish before they know what to print.
  • return on ad spend for a US conversion-optimized campaign focused on one of VistaPrint’s popular product categories.1.
  • lower cost per attributed order for a US conversion-optimized campaign focused on one of VistaPrint’s popular product categories, compared with the preceding click-focused campaign for that category.2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Small business owners preparing for a launch or an event often know what they want to accomplish before they know what to print. VistaPrint uses ChatGPT Ads to show how products like signs and branded merchandise can help them get the word out.

return on ad spend for a US conversion-optimized campaign focused on one of VistaPrint’s popular product categories.1.

lower cost per attributed order for a US conversion-optimized campaign focused on one of VistaPrint’s popular product categories, compared with the preceding click-focused campaign for that category.2.

For decades, VistaPrint has helped small businesses bring ideas to life, from business cards and signage to a wide range of branded merchandise. But small business needs do not always start with a specific product in mind. A customer may be launching a business, preparing for an event, refreshing their brand, or looking for ways to market themselves more effectively.

That creates an opportunity to reach customers as they explore what they need and evaluate the different ways to bring their ideas to life. It was this opportunity that drew VistaPrint to the ChatGPT Ads pilot.

“What excites us about ChatGPT is where it sits in the customer journey—at the point where intent is still forming. When a potential customer doesn’t yet know what they need, and they’re in a conversation working that out, that’s exactly where we want to be. Discovery is where we can help inform the decision, not just respond to it.”.

VistaPrint’s early campaigns leaned on product-oriented messaging. The team shifted the focus to what small business owners could do with them, like using signs to draw people to a booth or handing out branded merchandise at an event.

This became the foundation of an evolving playbook. Creative could help customers see how a product fit their needs; the team also wanted its campaign optimization to reflect what happened next. For VistaPrint, the business goal was to turn that interest into orders.

VistaPrint explored that next step with two successive US campaigns for one of its popular product categories. The first used click-focused bidding. In July 2026, the team rolled out a conversion-optimized campaign. VistaPrint selected ‘Order Created’ as the conversion event and paid per valid click.

Industry observers note that as the campaign learned from conversion data, the team evaluated performance and adjusted maximum bids. VistaPrint reported that cost per attributed order was approximately 90% lower in the conversion-optimized campaign than in the preceding click-focused campaign.2 The conversion-optimized campaign recorded a 5.9x return on ad spend.1.

Sources indicate that those results gave VistaPrint the confidence to expand the approach across its remaining US campaigns and into the UK, Canada, and Australia. The experience added a practical lesson to the team’s creative learning: allow time for conversion-focused bidding to learn, then keep evaluating performance as the campaign develops.

Product feeds added another way to connect customer needs with VistaPrint’s range. Alongside its standard campaigns, the team introduced catalog-based campaigns using product information from its feed to populate ads.

Sources indicate that “ChatGPT Ads isn’t about choosing between text or catalog formats—it’s about the synergy between the two and having a balanced campaign structure. While our standard campaigns allow us to engage in broader conversations about a customer’s business goals, our dynamic product feeds instantly provide them with the right products they are looking for.”.

In a recent development, vistaPrint used its catalog results to guide spend allocation and expanded feed campaigns to other markets. Its recommendation to other ecommerce advertisers is to invest in a clean, well-structured feed alongside creative tailored to the conversational context.

In a recent development, reaching upcoming customers was central to VistaPrint’s original goal for the channel. From July through September, a majority of the US site conversions VistaPrint traced to ChatGPT Ads came from new customers.3.

These results have given VistaPrint the confidence to expand its approach across campaigns and markets. For the team, the opportunity is to connect with small businesses as their ideas take shape—and help them discover the products that can bring those ideas to life.

Reach people as they explore options, compare choices, and make decisions in ChatGPT, with relevant ads that fit naturally into the experience.

Based on VistaPrint-reported platform-attributed sales for the US conversion-optimized campaign, July 8–August 4, 2026.

Kuken Industries searches 70 years of drawings in minutes

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kuken’s engineers use a tool built on the OpenAI API to find the drawing for a replacement part in 4.5 minutes, down from nearly an hour.
  • Projected reduction in hours spent searching for drawings each year.
  • According to recent reports, kuken Industries makes air conditioning and ventilation equipment for large buildings, shopping centers, and factories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kuken’s engineers use a tool built on the OpenAI API to find the drawing for a replacement part in 4.5 minutes, down from nearly an hour.

Projected reduction in hours spent searching for drawings each year.

Time to find a drawing, down from nearly an hour.

According to recent reports, kuken Industries makes air conditioning and ventilation equipment for large buildings, shopping centers, and factories. It holds one of the largest shares of Japan’s cooling tower market. These towers release heat from circulating water into the air, helping cool everything from large buildings and malls to equipment in data centers.

Industry observers note that when a cooling tower needs a replacement part, Kuken’s engineers turn to an archive of drawings that spans 70 years of installations. For a newer engineer, finding the right drawing often meant asking an experienced colleague where to look and how to read it. Kuken wanted newer engineers to be able to find those records themselves, learn from the decisions they contain, and spend more time figuring out how to make the repair.

It has been revealed that parts made today don’t always fit older cooling towers. Without the original drawing to show what was installed, engineers may have to design and manufacture a replacement from scratch.

A search by model or part name can turn up several drawings. Over more than 70 years, Kuken has adapted its equipment to individual customers, so specifications vary by customer and installation date. When the archive was on paper, a search could take half a day. Kuken later digitized the archive, but engineers still had to know which name or number to look up and where to find the file. Newer engineers in particular spent time piecing those details together.

It has been revealed that kuken wanted engineers at every experience level to be able to search the archive on their own. As it explored how AI might help, Kuken connected with Recursive, a Japanese AI startup and an official OpenAI partner.

The two companies built the search system and its field app together, drawing on Kuken’s archive and input from its engineers. They tested several AI models on a range of drawings to see how accurately each could extract details and at what cost. OpenAI’s models performed well on both measures, and the OpenAI API gave the team the flexibility to build search directly into the app.

Conversations with field engineers shaped how the search works. Engineers can enter a drawing or part number, or upload an image or PDF of a drawing or parts list.

In a recent development, pasting in a screenshot of the list saves engineers from entering each number by hand. The app reads the part numbers and returns possible matches, including drawings for similar designs. To find the right drawing, engineers check the tower’s specifications and records of past replacements.

Kuken reports the following results from using and testing the search tool.

Kuken expects the tool to cut the hours spent searching for drawings by about 90% over a year.

Experienced engineers use some of the time they save to mentor newer colleagues.

Engineers can review drawings in the app, reducing printing costs.

According to recent reports, engineers now spend less time looking for a drawing and more time studying it. Both newer engineers and veterans say that gives them room to consider design improvements and explore ideas they previously had little time to pursue.

Newer engineers can now handle a wider range of jobs on their own. Experienced colleagues who used to guide them through each search have more time to teach and to take on engineering work of their own.

Kuken is also developing a tool to check drawings prepared by its partners. Today, engineers compare each drawing with the specifications by eye, looking for details or quantities that don’t match. Kuken wants the tool to flag those differences so engineers can review drawings faster and catch mistakes they might otherwise miss.

According to Kuken, in prototype testing, about 90% of the concerns the AI flagged were genuine discrepancies. If the tool moves into production, Kuken expects it to substantially reduce the time engineers spend checking drawings.

Each drawing records decisions an engineer made for a particular installation. By making those decisions easier to find and understand, Kuken aims to pass that experience on to the next generation of engineers.

Breaking: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.
  • Recent findings suggest that for Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a new window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work.
  • CodeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.

Recent findings suggest that for Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a new window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every firm hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot notes.

CodeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship.

Sources indicate that according to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and Codex⁠ helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The manufacturer also uses Daybreak⁠ to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code. Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents.

It has been revealed that codeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot claims the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The firm went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis.

It has been revealed that the team evaluates new models against its own benchmark of known problems. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that GPT‑6 Astra⁠ caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark.

The benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” states Harjot.

Industry observers note that better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the organization use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers.

Sources indicate that when CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration.

Recent findings suggest that “Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot states. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves.

According to recent reports, by using Codex, Harjot says the manufacturer has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers. He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

Getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies.

The team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot indicates.

Recent findings suggest that the company has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing.

CodeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the company as code as much as possible,” Harjot notes.

In marketing, the company manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot says.

Sources indicate that codeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform.

The team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot claims the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says.

It has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the company ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their consumers and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security.

As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale.

The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

#45421. Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1273 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential challenges, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed.
  • Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.
  • Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential challenges, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.

Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.

Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.

Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the workload, the inference engine, and the centralized Control Room service.

The workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved safety case.

According to recent reports, the inference engine, or just engine, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload.

The Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output.

Control Room is integrated in the following way:.

When starting a new job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room.

Whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room.

Sources indicate that control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job.

The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation.

Sources indicate that job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running.

Industry observers note that the workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request.

It has been revealed that control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests.

The request includes the job_id. This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room.

Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run.

Sources indicate that the job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request.

The model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work.

Sources indicate that A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running.

We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running.

The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the upcoming inference request, passing along the same job ID.

Recent findings suggest that when the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request.

The engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs.

All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A monitor is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent DNS-related incident⁠(opens in a upcoming window) was caught by a monitor.

Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way:.

If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job.

In a recent development, in this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated.

Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from any model running on any engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output.

The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly.

According to recent reports, workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code.

We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

In a recent development, finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days.

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, we're⁠ hiring⁠!

Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.
  • As Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them.
  • Sources indicate that cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.

Lower mean time to remediate vulnerabilities.

As Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them. Remediation work is complex and spans multiple teams. It requires contextual understanding of a firm’s environment: how could an attacker exploit a vulnerability, which business systems are at stake, and what changes can be made safely.

Sources indicate that cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks. The factories are designed to help defenders move at machine speed, in response to the acceleration in vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

The manufacturer’s AI agents combine GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 with its enterprise context and controls to handle investigation through verified remediation. The agents assess exposures, execute permitted changes, and confirm the risk has been eliminated. Cogent also conducts internal research with Cyber and Daybreak, exploring attack paths and defensive capabilities.

For each customer, Cogent’s Context Engine maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies. Specialized background agents continuously reconcile information across security tools and systems, giving investigation and remediation agents a shared understanding of the environment.

GPT‑6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning for that work. This enables what Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO of Cogent, describes as a “memory harness for the enterprise.” He says, “We don’t have to relearn what the world looks like every time a new task happens.” Reusing context reduces latency, inference costs, and inconsistent results.

Cogent’s Agent Policies define each enterprise’s permitted changes and approval requirements, and its policy-enforcement engine, TRACE, checks tool calls against the policies before execution. The checks are deterministic and require no separate model inference.

According to recent reports, an Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or permit bounded autonomous remediation.

When critical security flaws known as PHP2Shell were disclosed in PHP, a programming language used to run websites, customers turned to the Cyber Defense Factories that Cogent had already deployed in their environments.

Sources indicate that GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Astra provided the deep reasoning for investigation and remediation planning. Using Cogent’s context layer, agents identified affected systems, assessed exposure, and developed intends that accounted for application dependencies and operational constraints. Then they orchestrated fixes using customer-defined approval and execution workflows and verified the resolution.

In a recent development, cogent reports that customers are using its Cyber Defense Factories to resolve vulnerabilities faster and expand investigation capacity. With Cogent, a Fortune 1000 automotive customer reduced its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer achieved 5× vulnerability-triage throughput.

Global electronic trading platform MarketAxess leverages Cogent to help strengthen its risk-based approach to exposure management. “Cogent brings together vulnerability data, business context, security controls, and attack path analysis to help us validate real exposures and prioritize remediation where it matters most. What stands out is how rapidly the Cogent team responds to emerging threats and turns our feedback into practical capabilities,” says Vijay Bala, CISO, MarketAxess.

Cogent continuously evaluates closed-source and open-source alternatives and reports stronger reasoning on long-running security tasks, higher fidelity, fewer hallucinations on technical codebases, and more reliable execution with OpenAI models. The models can chain tool calls sequentially and in parallel while retaining context across remediation workflows.

Cogent prioritizes reasoning quality for complex investigations and cost for more straightforward work. It uses GPT‑6.1 Sol for general execution and GPT‑5.6 for routine vulnerability-management tasks where advanced reasoning is less critical.

Using OpenAI models has also reduced the supporting software Cogent needs to build for remediation and patching. “A lot of the work that we had to do at the harness level is no longer required,” Geng notes. He also shared that OpenAI APIs have “streamlined request routing and agent orchestration, significantly reducing internal engineering overhead and accelerating our time-to-market for complex security workflows.”.

Most of Cogent’s engineers also choose Codex for development. Geng says they’re more productive pairing Codex with OpenAI models vs. using the same models in an open-source coding environment. “Codex just comes with tools that we don’t have to build ourselves,” says Geng.

Recent findings suggest that through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, Cogent receives technical support for its internal red-teaming and attack-path research. Daybreak Red, an access tier within Daybreak, provides the team with specialized OpenAI models for authorized offensive and vulnerability research. “Good defense requires good offense,” Geng says.

Sources indicate that cogent plans to expand its capabilities as the key partner for enterprises to build their own Cyber Defense Factories. Its roadmap includes increasingly autonomous remediation, broadening the range and complexity of fixes agents can execute, from straightforward configuration changes to multi-step workflows spanning different enterprise systems.

According to recent reports, the company is also developing autonomous discovery and validation. Its goal is a closed-loop system that finds and eliminates risk while continuously learning from every vulnerability to improve future investigations and fixes.

Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.
  • Sources indicate that for freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope.
  • According to recent reports, the stakes are substantial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.

Sources indicate that for freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

According to recent reports, the stakes are substantial. Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a upcoming window) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

Freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that the mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

Sources indicate that these activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.

It has been revealed that many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the remaining 20 work categories indicated the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people at the moment use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

It has been revealed that each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis shows the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.

It has been revealed that by late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

Sources indicate that some clients asked for AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21.

Although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous Work at the Frontier papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Sources indicate that because freelance projects turn over rapidly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a upcoming job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

Recent findings suggest that the findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.

With the OpenAI API and models, Singapore Airlines improves customer support, travel discovery, and employee work, doubling CSAT for the Kris customer service chatbot.

Increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT) with AI-powered Kris chatbot.

Reduction in average handling time for customer service representatives using AI-assisted tools.

Growth in Flight Recommender monthly users over the past year.

AI is becoming part of how Singapore Airlines serves customers, empowers employees, and builds technology. The airline uses the OpenAI API for customer-facing experiences and OpenAI models inside Jarvis, its governed internal AI platform for employees. It also uses OpenAI models in its software development workflows to deliver more personalized service, improve productivity, and help teams build more efficiently.

Across these deployments, Singapore Airlines pairs OpenAI models with orchestration, internal data controls, validation, and human review, giving teams a consistent way to bring AI into production workflows responsibly.

It has been revealed that one of Singapore Airlines’ most visible AI applications is Kris, its customer-facing chatbot. After moving Kris from a traditional dialog-flow system to an LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API, Singapore Airlines saw a 2x increase in customer satisfaction.

Industry observers note that alongside that, the airline deployed AI-assisted tools for customer service representatives, including OpenAI API-powered call summarization, so that representatives spend less time on after-call work and more time on the customer. Singapore Airlines saw an approximately 10% reduction in average handling time for its customer service representatives.

It has been revealed that in the earlier dialog-flow based chatbot design, every topic had to be mapped manually, and every flow had to be written in advance. That made coverage difficult to scale. If an intent was missing, the conversation was more likely to end up requiring support from a customer service representative, even when the customer’s request could have been handled through self-service.

Sources indicate that singapore Airlines moved Kris to a fully LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API. Instead of depending on predefined flows, the chatbot can interpret customer intent in natural language, ground answers in a knowledge base, manage multi-topic conversations, and hand over to a customer service representative with the relevant context when needed.

Today, customers use Kris for general queries, special requests, real-time flight disruption information, and selected transactional workflows. Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand its capabilities to include booking changes, baggage transactions, and more complex agentic interactions.

Flight Recommender lets customers describe the trip they want in natural language instead of repeatedly adjusting filters, dates, and destinations. Usage has grown nearly 3x over the past year.

Built on the OpenAI API, Flight Recommender uses an orchestration layer connected to fare and availability data. It interprets customer intent, calls the relevant tools, and returns personalized travel recommendations in natural language.

Industry observers note that the team has also implemented guardrails for input and output validation, malicious or inappropriate query handling, hallucination reduction, PII handling, and authenticated access to only the context required for each query. Singapore Airlines is preparing to expand the experience into a more conversational chatbot interaction, where customers can keep refining travel ideas rather than restarting a search.

Industry observers note that beyond customer-facing experiences, Singapore Airlines is also using OpenAI models in parts of the software development lifecycle to help teams proposal, refine, test, and review work more efficiently. Across selected software development lifecycle activities, teams have achieved productivity gains of up to 20%.

AI now runs through the entire delivery lifecycle and not just coding. Teams use generative AI models to support requirements refinement, stakeholder-session analysis, product specifications, edge-case identification, test-case creation, architecture review, and the breakdown of complex work into smaller, more testable tasks.

For one commercial feature, the team used the OpenAI API to challenge assumptions, identify ambiguous requirements and surface edge cases before development begins. Once those were well-defined, AI helped translate them into design options, implementation looks, test cases and then code generation.

During deployment and beyond, AI also helps to interpret how the system is behaving in production, and flagging problems that might otherwise go unnoticed. With AI active at every step of the workflow, team members have shifted from producing every artifact themselves, to directing, reviewing and validating what AI produces throughout the delivery lifecycle. This means they can focus on work that truly requires human judgement, such as prioritization, architecture, governance and stakeholder outcomes.

More broadly, OpenAI models are helping Singapore Airlines improve requirements quality, test coverage, and conformance with internal standards. Teams use these workflows to generate edge cases for testing, review architecture looks, and support human validation before work moves further through the development lifecycle.

Beyond engineering teams, Singapore Airlines is making AI accessible across the business through Jarvis, its internal AI platform. Powered by OpenAI models, Jarvis gives employees a governed way to use AI in their day-to-day work, from summarizing documents to creating custom workflows.

Recent findings suggest that employees use Jarvis to work across PDFs, Word documents, Excel files, PowerPoint decks, and other file types in a secure environment, while creating custom workflows and lightweight knowledge bases for their day-to-day work. Today, more than 60% of Singapore Airlines employees are using Jarvis monthly with adoption continuing to increase.

For Kris, the next phase is deeper self-service, with more transactional capabilities that help customers resolve requests directly in chat. Flight Recommender is moving toward a more conversational travel discovery experience, where customers can refine ideas over multiple turns rather than restarting a search.

It has been revealed that with Jarvis available across the business, Singapore Airlines is focused on helping more employees put AI to work in their day-to-day roles. Together with its customer-facing innovations, this is helping the airline build a future where AI makes travel more seamless, employees more productive, and the business more responsive to changing needs.

  • Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Drawing on newly introduced ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.

AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the OECD’s Andreas Schleicher⁠(opens in a fresh window), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems.

Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions.

This report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence.

Three early patterns are emerging from this work:.

Country partnerships offer context-specific lessons. Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale.

Recent findings suggest that closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent. Latest research from ThinkYoung,⁠(opens in a new window) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use.

Recent findings suggest that early benefits for teachers are clear. Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area.

Recent findings suggest that our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow.

We are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter.

According to recent reports, at OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems.

Recent findings suggest that the choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Upgrade on November 19, 2026: Ecommerce and online service businesses based outside the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that we’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a latest way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT.

Upgrade on November 19, 2026: Ecommerce and online service businesses based outside the U.S. are now eligible to claim their business and publish agents in ChatGPT.

Originally published on November 10, 2026.

Industry observers note that we’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a latest way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through Business Hub⁠(opens in a new window), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with owners via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S.

Together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star.

In Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, update key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a new way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details.

Any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog.

Business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share.

It has been revealed that we’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share consumers’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds.

After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings.

In a recent development, when a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information.

For customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers.

Industry observers note that businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent⁠ and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses.

Business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories here⁠.

It has been revealed that as people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we plan to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs.

Recent findings suggest that as the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.

Learn more and⁠ claim your business in ChatGPT.⁠.

Industry observers note that in collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, bringing free, hands-on ChatGPT workshops to five U.S. cities during National Family Caregivers Month.

Recent findings suggest that caregiving often means juggling schedules, keeping track of information, and finding support while balancing work and family life. During National Family Caregivers Month, we’re helping caregivers gain AI skills that can make some of those everyday tasks easier, giving them more time to focus on the people they care for.

Sources indicate that on November 10, OpenAI Academy, in collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, is hosting the AI Skills Jam for Caregivers & Community Health: a free, in-person learning experience designed to help caregivers use ChatGPT confidently, safely, and practically. These nationwide events will bring together participants across five U.S. cities, including individual and family caregivers, caregiver support organizations, and people living with chronic or serious health conditions:.

In a recent development, an OpenAI analysis estimates that more than 40 million weekly ChatGPT messages about healthcare in the U.S. ask about healthcare for someone else1. At the workshops, participants will explore how ChatGPT can help with resource navigation, peer support, and caregiver support, including how to:.

organize caregiver schedules and checklists.

turn trusted educational resources into plain-language materials.

prepare support group discussion guides.

Participants will also learn how to use AI responsibly, including protecting personal information and understanding the limits of these tools. Participants will also learn when to consult healthcare professionals and how AI tools should complement, not replace, medical, legal, or financial advice. OpenAI facilitators and mentors will offer hands-on support throughout the workshops. No coding or technical background is required.

Industry observers note that the Jam brings this learning into local communities, where caregivers can practice alongside peers and share the everyday challenges they hope these tools can help address. Our partners bring deep expertise and experience supporting people living with serious illness and their families. Their perspectives, together with those of caregivers themselves, will help connect the day’s learning to the needs of each community.

In a recent development, the AI Skills Jam is part of OpenAI Academy’s broader work to make AI practical and accessible to everyone. It builds on previous events we’ve hosted with nonprofits, small businesses, K–12 educators, and older adults.

According to recent reports, we are grateful to Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, American Diabetes Association®, and the caregivers and community health organizations joining us across the country. Their questions, ideas, and experiences will help shape future learning resources and ensure these tools are useful in the daily work of supporting others.

This is from a privacy-preserving ChatGPT usage estimate for October 9–29, 2026.

Latest Update: JioStar’s chief architect on AI discovery at 500M-user scale

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A conversation with Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect at JioStar.
  • Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.
  • According to recent reports, jioStar operates entertainment and live-sports platforms used by more than 500 million consumers and has supported as many as 72.5 million concurrent live-sports viewers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A conversation with Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect at JioStar.

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

According to recent reports, jioStar operates entertainment and live-sports platforms used by more than 500 million consumers and has supported as many as 72.5 million concurrent live-sports viewers. At that scale, AI has to be fast, reliable, and ready for production.

It has been revealed that using the OpenAI API, JioStar built a conversational video and cricket-stat discovery assistant into JioHotstar. Viewers can speak naturally to find movies and indicates, historical highlights, live-match moments, or cricket statistics, with results returned through a visual, conversational experience.

At OpenAI’s Executive Summit in Singapore, Sidharth Sharma, OpenAI’s Head of Go-to-Market for ASEAN, spoke with Vijay Seshadri—Chief Architect, JioStar, about building the experience for more than 15 languages in about eight weeks, and the lessons for leaders taking AI from demo to production.

Content discovery has evolved very little in the past 25 years. Recommendations were the last major shift. Much of what followed has been an iteration of the same idea.

Sources indicate that but choosing what to watch is deeply personal. A person might say, “I’m feeling sad. Show me something that will cheer me up.” Even that simple request contains a lot of nuance. What kind of sad? What usually cheers that person up? Do they want comedy, comfort viewing or something completely distracting?

A traditional recommendation system may struggle to understand that moment. Conversation gives the viewer a way to explain it. We call this a voice-visual interface.

We began working through the concept in October and November, with a major cricket tournament coming in February. We had roughly two months and two very different audiences: entertainment viewers and cricket fans.

Industry observers note that an entertainment viewer might say, “It’s Friday evening—surprise me,” or describe a movie without knowing its title. Sports viewers may want a more specific update, like fall of wickets, a series of sixes, or the match in which a player scored a certain number of runs. Cricket experts may want statistics about every ball.

These are very different discovery problems. We worked on bringing entertainment, sports moments and detailed cricket statistics into one experience, across multiple languages, in a very short period.

According to recent reports, very early, we framed the problem as a three-way tradeoff among accuracy, latency, and cost. Every engineering decision had to balance all three at once.

Recent findings suggest that voice made that especially key. More than 60% of our owners use voice rather than text: people prefer to say what they want to watch. The response still has to be relevant, fast, and economically viable at scale.

In a recent development, I think about it in two parts: an evaluation framework and a validation layer. Before production, the evaluation framework should prompt changes. In production, a feedback loop should turn customer behavior and failures into new eval cases.

That flywheel can become self-amplified, but it is extremely difficult to get right.

Domain experts are essential. For sports-statistics evals, we worked with people such as sports-magazine editors who understood what serious fans might ask. You cannot begin with a prompt alone; you need to seed the system with deep human expertise.

One thing we got right was the team. We started with a small team of data scientists and engineers around a clear problem statement. OpenAI’s forward-deployed engineers worked alongside us to further identify the few things we absolutely had to get right.

According to recent reports, the first was scope. A voice or text interface lets users ask almost anything, so we began by deciding what the system should not answer. Guardrails came first.

For evals, we began with a seed dataset and used models to expand it with more variation. We created what you might now call a maker-checker pattern: one model helped determine how to answer a question, while another acted as a validator—an LLM as judge—with a competing objective.

That raised another question: who tests the judge? Designing the validator was itself an evaluation problem. Codex helped the team accelerate work such as generating eval cases and updating the system, but faster building did not remove the need for judgment and validation.

I would invest earlier in production monitoring for model efficacy.

Traditional infrastructure measures such as P99 latency remain notable, but they are not enough. You also need to monitor model efficacy in production.

In a recent development, first, there is a large gap between what technology can do and the reality inside an enterprise. If your company has not matched every frontier-model announcement, you are not alone.

Recent findings suggest that second, keep focusing on outcomes rather than activity. It is easy to mistake visible motion for meaningful progress, particularly when companies emphasize input metrics. Lines of code generated, for example, do not tell you whether you created meaningful value.

Finally, most enterprises underestimate the human skill and agency required. This cannot be only a generic skilling program. Leaders need people who can apply these tools with judgment. Give a strong engineer a tool like Codex and the impact can multiply; without the judgment to validate production systems, the risk multiplies too.

Industry observers note that you have a rocket in your hands. Especially in production systems, you need validation and guardrails, and you need to give the keys to the right people.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in the past year, more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a year of ChatGPT Plus at no cost after being offered free access by OpenAI.
  • The effort started with veterans who work here at OpenAI, people who use these tools every day and know firsthand how challenging the transition can be.
  • Sources indicate that leaving the military often means stepping into an unfamiliar job market and working out how years of service translate into a civilian role.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in the past year, more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a year of ChatGPT Plus at no cost after being offered free access by OpenAI. That milestone gives us a chance to look at how veterans are using AI to prepare for civilian careers and to figure out what comes next for themselves and their families.

The effort started with veterans who work here at OpenAI, people who use these tools every day and know firsthand how challenging the transition can be. Beyond the free access, OpenAI Academy and our community partners have hosted more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, with seven more⁠(opens in a fresh window) scheduled before the year ends.

Sources indicate that leaving the military often means stepping into an unfamiliar job market and working out how years of service translate into a civilian role. Many veterans are turning to ChatGPT to organize their job search, rehearse for interviews, and explore paths they hadn’t considered.

Air Force veteran Tilak Bhatnagar⁠(opens in a fresh window) used his free year to prepare for a dozen interviews, find the right words to describe his military experience to civilian employers, and weigh competing job offers. Along the way, those conversations helped him clarify what he actually wanted from life after active duty.

In a recent development, he ultimately took a role at a tech organization. What he valued most was being able to pick up where he left off, returning to the same thread about his background, goals, and constraints. As he put it, “each conversation built on the last.”.

Sadarian Bell⁠(opens in a upcoming window), also an Air Force veteran, started planning more than a year before he left the service. He used ChatGPT to map out his transition and to turn nearly a decade of military healthcare experience into a civilian résumé.

To prepare for interviews, he practiced out loud using ChatGPT voice mode, working through one question at a time until his answers felt natural. “It has genuinely become my career coach,” Sadarian remarked, though he also learned to recognize when he’d had enough help and could trust his own judgment.

For Navy veteran Kelli Ramirez⁠(opens in a upcoming window), the transition was a chance to chase a long-held dream: becoming a published author. She’d already invested in a book-writing course to sharpen her craft, and ChatGPT filled in the gaps. “ChatGPT helped me organize ideas, ask questions about publishing, and work through the Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing process,” she remarked.

Kelli has since published two books, which she says “reflect my desire to help women approach technology with confidence and, for those who share my Christian faith, with wisdom grounded in that faith.”.

Not everyone arrives confident about using AI tools, which is why OpenAI Academy gives veterans, transitioning servicemembers, and military spouses a place to learn alongside people who understand what they’re going through.

OpenAI recently wrapped our first six-event Academy series with Veterans Forge⁠(opens in a new window), focused on helping veterans and military families use ChatGPT to work toward their goals. That pilot, together with workshops alongside AI Collective Hampton Roads and NPower, is shaping what we offer veterans next.

At one workshop in Reston, Virginia⁠(opens in a new window), nearly 100 veterans and active-duty servicemembers⁠(opens in a new window) explored ways to put AI to work. Participant Ryan Kaono-Wedemeyer⁠(opens in a new window) learned to start by writing out a detailed account of his military experience, then asking AI to help shape it into a civilian résumé.

Instructor Erin Marie⁠(opens in a new window) helped participants build custom GPTs to support their transitions, and watched people who walked in skeptical begin finding ways the tools could genuinely help them.

According to recent reports, in Louisville, Kentucky, more than 80 Legionnaires⁠(opens in a fresh window) attended three AI training sessions at the American Legion’s national convention. For those who can’t make it to an event, our online veterans collection⁠(opens in a new window) and 100 chats for veterans⁠(opens in a new window) offer examples to try on your own.

We’re continuing this work with partners across the country through the rest of the year:.

November 12: NPower event in St. Louis⁠(opens in a new window).

November 14: Nashville event with Veterans Forge and Wounded Warrior Project⁠(opens in a new window).

November 17: 30-minute virtual session⁠(opens in a fresh window).

November 19: NPower event in Dallas⁠(opens in a latest window).

November 21: NPower event in San Antonio⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Sources indicate that our goal is to help veterans and military families carry the skills they built in service into whatever work they choose next. We’re grateful to ID.me⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) for helping servicemembers and veterans access the free-year offer, and to our community partners for making these events possible.

This Veterans Day, OpenAI thanks veterans for their service and for contributing to their communities.

See if you’re eligible for a free year of ChatGPT Plus.⁠(opens in a new window).

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

Recent findings suggest that gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a new window) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”.

It has been revealed that when ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

Recent findings suggest that governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

Leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Sources indicate that gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into newly introduced technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”.

Sources indicate that to help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins) using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

According to recent reports, I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to enhancement files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

With a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s notable to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Industry observers note that pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

It has been revealed that the opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.
