General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1535 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • The first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally indicates "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

It has been revealed that on the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

It has been revealed that image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

In a recent development, ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

Industry observers note that no dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

It has been revealed that training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

Sources indicate that if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now provides a Primary Endpoint, a DNS name that always resolves to the current primary DB instance in a replica configuration.
  • Sources indicate that with Primary Endpoint, you can run planned switchovers, such as disaster recovery drills, to replicas in the same AWS Region or to cross-Region replicas without changing your application configuration.
  • Every RDS for Oracle Enterprise Edition DB instance has a Primary Endpoint at no additional charge, and you don't have to create it.

Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now provides a Primary Endpoint, a DNS name that always resolves to the current primary DB instance in a replica configuration. When you switch over to an Oracle replica, Amazon RDS points the Primary Endpoint to the fresh primary DB instance, so you don't need to change your application connection strings. Previously, after each switchover, you had to update connection strings or DNS records to point to the new primary DB instance, which often required change approvals and coordination across teams.

Sources indicate that with Primary Endpoint, you can run planned switchovers, such as disaster recovery drills, to replicas in the same AWS Region or to cross-Region replicas without changing your application configuration. If your applications connect through the Primary Endpoint, you don't need to update their connection strings after the switchover.

Every RDS for Oracle Enterprise Edition DB instance has a Primary Endpoint at no additional charge, and you don't have to create it. The Primary Endpoint is provided in addition to the instance endpoint, so your existing applications aren't affected.

In a recent development, primary Endpoint is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. To learn more, see Using the Primary Endpoint for Amazon RDS for Oracle in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device.
  • LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • Sources indicate that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Sources indicate that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

Sources indicate that we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

Sources indicate that for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

According to recent reports, edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

Sources indicate that GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

Sources indicate that serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

Industry observers note that the port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, flows in AWS Quick now lets users build, run, and refine automations for themselves and their teams, all through conversation. Users describe a process in chat, and Quick builds the flow, with no coding needed.

It has been revealed that flows can now orchestrate agents, skills, and tools, with access to structured data, knowledge, and apps. A flow can pull answers from the business data a team already reports on, produce ready-to-share documents, spreadsheets, and presentations, and save the results to a team space. Flows also support longer-running workflows and larger volumes of data.

Upcoming deterministic steps help keep results consistent, and validations check each step's output against rules the user sets, such as requiring a summary table in a report, before the flow continues. For example, an accounts payable team can build a flow that uses agents to read invoices and match them to purchase orders, and deterministic steps to check totals and catch duplicates.

Consumers can now run flows wherever they work, across desktop, web, and mobile. In the desktop app, flows can work with local files and complete tasks in the browser. In the mobile app, users can start flows and check on them on the go.

These updates are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Quick is available.

To learn more, see Flows in AWS Quick in the AWS Quick User Guide and the AWS Quick product page.

Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Sources indicate that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

It has been revealed that add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Sources indicate that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Industry observers note that for edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Sources indicate that black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

In a recent development, A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

In a recent development, FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

It has been revealed that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Industry observers note that every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

According to recent reports, the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Sources indicate that text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Industry observers note that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps reveals how the image takes shape:.

Recent findings suggest that the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are latest to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

In a recent development, get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

Industry observers note that built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎.

According to recent reports, web Search on Amazon Bedrock, the tool that grounds AI agents and applications in cited, current web information, now supports five new languages, plus non-US English, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock: Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Japanese. Agents serving consumers in these languages get results that draw on local-language sources.

Industry observers note that we are also introducing a upcoming optional country field that biases results toward sources from a specific country - just pass an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, such as “JP” or “DE”. This is useful for agents that serve users in multiple countries, for questions whose answer depends on the user's actual or preferred location (e.g., local regulations, prices or public officials), and for surfacing regional sources.

It has been revealed that both the expanded language support and the optional  country field are available today in every Region where Web Search is offered: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland) for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and US Regions for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock. Queries are processed in the Region you call, helping organizations meet data residency requirements. Existing customers get the new language capabilities automatically, with no code changes, and pricing is the same in every language.

To get started with Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, checkout the developer guide and the web search product page.

#45283. Breaking: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3181 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.
  • By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff.
  • Sources indicate that the staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.

By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff.

Sources indicate that the staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

Industry observers note that as we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories.

Sources indicate that 1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

According to recent reports, 3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:.

Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it.

We tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

Sources indicate that 4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

According to recent reports, 5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

In a recent development, 6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

Performance Factory consists of a task service, dispatch loop, cloud execution, and subscriptions.

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

Recent findings suggest that each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

According to recent reports, A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

Sources indicate that once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

According to recent reports, the agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation, root caused, fix proposed, and resolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

Recent findings suggest that when one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

The Regression Workflow’s steps include finding the root cause, proposing a fix, reviewing and deploying, and verifying recovery.

In a recent development, finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The perf-forensics skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

It has been revealed that once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

Recent findings suggest that early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. If a rollout caused the slowdown, did similar requests that weren’t exposed stay healthy? If the suspected change was rolled back, did the affected metric recover?

Industry observers note that in one investigation, an agent traced failing ChatGPT conversations to errors in image downloads and marked the cause as found. The Codex reviewer noticed that the internal service responsible for locating files had already recovered while image requests were still failing. The diagnosis did not explain the continuing failures, so the AI reviewer reopened the investigation and recorded what still needed to be established.

Industry observers note that we’ve had success breaking larger jobs into focused Codex turns. In a manual review of 100 root cause suggestions, we graded 70% as accurate, with 30% needing further refinement or not fully establishing causality. In the Regression Workflow, different turns investigate regressions, challenge diagnoses, and propose fixes to increase accuracy numbers through checks and balances.

According to recent reports, once the diagnosis passes adversarial review, the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request. An engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it. We’ve put a significant amount of work into making this handoff as easy as possible. Each task has a report with an automatically generated summary of the regression, its impact, the root cause, and the proposed fix. We’ve tuned these summaries to be easy to scan, including metrics time series, CPU flame graphs, and traces to help engineers quickly understand the findings and inspect the evidence. Engineers can edit the PR directly or use the diagnosis to write their own fix. If they leave comments on the PR, the workflow wakes an agent to address them.

An example task report for a regression demonstrates key details, root cause, and proposed fix.

According to recent reports, after an engineer deploys the fix, the workflow wakes an agent to check whether performance has returned to its earlier baseline. If it has, the agent marks the task as resolved. If performance has only partially recovered, the agent resolves the original regression and opens a newly introduced task for the remaining slowdown, which may have a different cause. If there’s no improvement, the agent records what happened and sends the regression back for investigation.

Getting fixes right has been harder than finding the cause. For example, we’ve seen cases where the agent-proposed changes are more complicated than necessary or introduce new issues. Similar to the root cause step, we added an adversarial review of each proposed fix to check whether they address the root cause and help catch bugs or unintended consequences. Some fixes also require higher level architectural decisions. For example, adding a cache might improve performance but introduce stale data. Changes like these benefit from guidance from an engineer who knows the service and can weigh the tradeoffs.

It has been revealed that we’re building an evaluation and improvement loop using these cases. By comparing the fixes agents propose with the changes engineers ultimately merge, we can better understand where proposals fall short, build evals, and improve the workflow. We’re also working on using synthetic performance tests so agents can measure proposed fixes and revise them before asking an engineer for review. We’re also exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop.

Sources indicate that building and running the Performance Factory has taught us a lot about developing and operating agent workflows in production. Here are some lessons for teams building their own agentic workflows.

The raw output from a Codex investigation can be a wall of text that’s hard to parse. It takes effort to figure out what the agent is claiming and track down the graphs to see whether the data backs it up. We want engineers to spend their attention on decisions rather than reconstructing the agent’s work.

Recent findings suggest that agents can investigate more regressions than a team has time to read about. Our first version gave engineers a UI full of findings, but someone still had to decide which information mattered. One regression can also appear as several incidents across alerts, monitors, and channels. The workflow now links related incidents, groups them by the metrics teams care about, and ranks their estimated impact. Engineers can focus on adding context, weighing tradeoffs, and deciding what to ship.

According to recent reports, updating an investigation skill or upgrading the model can make the agent better at diagnosing some cases and worse at others, so we need to test their impact before updating them. We test two things separately: 1) how well the agent investigates and 2) how useful its summaries are to engineers.

It has been revealed that for investigations, we backtest against past production incidents. We turn those incidents into a suite of test cases we can rerun when we change the skill. A Codex agent attempts to investigate and resolve the incident, and we compare the agent’s behavior to the actual past resolution data. Each case starts with a fresh Codex investigator and the original signal, stripped of details that might give away the answer.

Historical tests need care. Metrics and traces expire, while evidence collected after recovery can give away the cause. A test is only useful if we understand what evidence the investigator could see. The agent can inspect code and query production telemetry within set limits. It cannot use saved memories (notes from earlier investigations), read the incident writeup, or see results from previous runs. We also inspect its transcript afterward for information that might have spoiled the test.

Industry observers note that we score when the problem began, how large it was, and which requests were affected. We also evaluate how the agent uses evidence to rank possible causes and explain what remains uncertain. An agent can get the timing right and still blame the wrong deployment, so we score those separately.

In a recent development, we evaluate task summaries using snapshots of saved tasks. These make particularly good backtests because summarization does not depend on external metrics or traces that expire. A separate grader checks whether an engineer unfamiliar with the system can understand what happened and why it matters, whether useful charts were kept, and whether the proposed next step is supported by the evidence.

It has been revealed that lastly, our agents need monitoring just as much as the services they investigate. A broken profiler or a missing permission can keep an agent from verifying what caused a slowdown. Those failures can be hard to spot in the final report, so we run an agent every day to look through messages and logs from recent runs for tool failures and access errors.

We use the Performance Factory to self-repair and fix the problems this check uncovers. When the same tool error blocks several investigations, the agent creates a task to fix it. If the cause is clear, an agent proposes a fix, and an engineer reviews the change and decides whether to merge it. After merging changes like this, we also use evals to check whether agents can get past the step that previously blocked them.

The Regression Workflow is just one instance of the agent factory pattern that moves tasks through explicit states. Agents advance the task when more work is ready; separate reviewers challenge the conclusions; engineers step in when the next decision requires judgment. Other workflows can reuse the same machinery with different states, instructions, and events.

From one workflow to many. The Performance Factory can coordinate agents across workflows, with agents in one workflow creating tasks for another.

It has been revealed that at the moment, our Regression Workflow starts when an alert fires. However, we’re working on more proactive ways for the Performance Factory to find slowdowns and optimizations even when no alert fires. We want agents to use the large amount of fine-grained performance data we already collect to spot regressions our alerts miss or discover optimizations. By comparing different kinds of data (batches of CPU and memory profiles, heap dumps, and request traces across releases), an agent might notice a small increase in CPU for a given request. It can then open a task in the Regression Workflow to trace the increase to its cause, implement a fix, and open a PR for an engineer to review.

In cases where we already know what to look for, we’re working to encode known signals into more Performance Factory workflows. Our service rightsizing skill, for example, helps agents spot autoscaling settings that keep more replicas running than a service needs. When we learn to recognize a pattern like that, we want to build and regularly run a workflow for it across all our services, constantly optimizing in a rapidly changing environment. With the Performance Factory, what an engineer learns from one slowdown can shape how we investigate and fix the next one, even months later in a different service.

Next time you’re using ChatGPT and notice a slowdown, there’s a good chance the Performance Factory is already figuring out why. Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We’re already exploring whether agents can do this themselves. As product development keeps accelerating with Codex, performance systems need to become increasingly autonomous and self-improving to keep up. Codex already helps us build ChatGPT faster. Now it’s helping us keep ChatGPT fast.

Special thanks to the team that built the Performance Factory, as well as our post contributors Brendan Gregg, Pieter Hooimeijer, Nick Cooper, and Louis Brandy.

Latest Update: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • In a recent development, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

In a recent development, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post reveals you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

In a recent development, meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

According to recent reports, the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Industry observers note that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

It has been revealed that A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

In a recent development, grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

Recent findings suggest that the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Sources indicate that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Sources indicate that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

Recent findings suggest that the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

It has been revealed that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

It has been revealed that the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server.

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:.

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:.

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:.

Industry observers note that the checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:.

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:.

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning demonstrates up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

In a recent development, note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

It has been revealed that the language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

It has been revealed that this is a significant model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/upcoming/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

Sources indicate that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Industry observers note that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Recent findings suggest that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

Industry observers note that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Recent findings suggest that the AWS Quick web app now brings the Quick desktop experience to your browser. Create, share, and use the same agents and skills as on desktop, with the same connectors. Industry observers note that additionally, agents you start or schedule from the web keep running after you close your browser. These updates are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and US East (N. Virginia).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

Recent findings suggest that one of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.

Industry observers note that medChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

It has been revealed that medChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:.

Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.

Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.

Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how swiftly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.

Sources indicate that predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.

Recent findings suggest that small chemical changes can produce different property profiles. The task asks models to connect the structures with evidence about their behavior.

In a recent development, before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.

MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.

In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.

In a recent development, these errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.

Figure 1. The same input, different molecules.

These selected answers for compound 17 show a correct reconstruction, a smaller ring, and disconnected fragments.

While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result demonstrates strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.

It has been revealed that we evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.

Figure 2. Performance versus token usage.

According to recent reports, each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Tokens include reasoning and the final answer.

The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Component performance versus token usage.

Sources indicate that astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.

Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.

Sources indicate that these results do not establish whether models can discover upcoming drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

Amazon CloudWatch Omni now supports collecting Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network (VNet) flow logs, and traces from Application Insights. Teams that run workloads on both AWS and Azure no longer need separate monitoring tools or custom pipelines to see their whole environment. Central operations, DevOps, and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams can now view Azure telemetry alongside their AWS telemetry in one place.

Recent findings suggest that to get started, connect a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to your AWS account and Region. You can choose the telemetry types, subscriptions, Azure regions, resource types, and tags to collect. Azure telemetry lands in Amazon CloudWatch, and Omni spaces can monitor applications and infrastructure across cloud providers. For example, during an incident you can trace a slow request from an Azure-hosted service to its AWS dependencies without switching consoles. You can set up the connectors in the Amazon CloudWatch Omni console or with the AWS CLI.

Azure telemetry collection is available in all Azure Public Regions and can be ingested to all regions where CloudWatch Omni is available. To get started, visit the  CloudWatch Omni User Guide  and for pricing visit pricing page.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
